# Investigating the mediating role of TPACK on teachers’ AI competency and their teaching performance in higher education

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

## Xiao Tan , Gary Cheng [\*,1](#computers-and-education-artificial-intelligence) [,](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-5614-3348) Man Ho Ling

_Department of Mathematics and Information Technology, The Education University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China_

## ARTICLE INFO ABSTRACT

### _Keywords:_ The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in education has significantly influenced teachers’ pro-

AI competency fessional development. While AI offers substantial support for teaching practices and serves as a powerful TPACK instructional aid, it also places greater demands on teachers, prompting an urgent need for role transformation Teaching performance

and skill enhancement. Therefore, the interplay among teachers’ AI competency, technological pedagogical 

Higher education

content knowledge (TPACK), and teaching performance has emerged as a critical area of research. This study employed a mixed-methods approach, combining questionnaire surveys with classroom observations, to assess the AI competency, TPACK levels, and teaching performance of 247 university teachers. Structural equation modelling (SEM) was used to analyze their relationships among the core constructs. The results revealed that teachers’ AI competency positively predicted their TPACK levels, which in turn positively predicted teaching performance. Furthermore, TPACK was found to mediate the relationship between AI competency and teaching performance. Theoretically, this study elucidates the interconnections among teachers’ AI competency, TPACK, and teaching performance, with a particular emphasis on the mediating role of TPACK. Practically, the findings offer implications for the design of professional development programmes aimed at strengthening teachers’ AI competency, as well as for the development of data-informed teaching performance evaluation systems. These insights contribute to improving instructional quality and supporting teachers’ continuous professional growth in 

the era of AI.

This is an open access article under the CC BY-NC license ([http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by- nc/4.0/)](http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/). increasingly expected not only to master the functional use of AI tools, but also to develop the pedagogical capacity to meaningfully integrate these tools into lesson planning, instruction, and assessment (Ahmed et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2020; Grajeda et al., 2023). Emerging research highlights a paradigmatic shift in teaching profession from knowledge transmission to learning facilitation, which calls for greater technolog- ical literacy and pedagogical adaptability (Celik, 2023; Meylani, 2024; Nazaretsky et al., 2022). To respond to this transformation, teachers must strengthen their capabilities across technological, pedagogical, and teaching practice domains to remain effective within AI-enhanced learning environments.

In terms of technological competency, teachers must acquire the technical skills necessary to effectively operate a range of AI tools, such as chatbots, automated assessment systems, and intelligent learning platforms, in order to facilitate the broader integration of AI into educational contexts (Chen et al., 2020; Holmes et al., 2023; Tan et al., 2025; Zawacki-Richter et al., 2019). Empirical research has consistently highlighted technological competency as a critical determinant of teachers’ ability to harness AI tools to support instruction and enhance student learning (Ahmed et al., 2022). For example, Mbambo and Du Plessis (2024) emphasized the importance of equipping teachers with sufficient technical knowledge to critically evaluate and apply AI tools, ensuring their appropriateness, integrity, and reliability in educational assessment. Beyond operational proficiency, teachers must also develop a critical awareness of the ethical and practical implications of AI in education (Chan, 2023; Fassbender, 2024; Williams, 2024). This in- cludes the ability to assess potential risks related to AI adoption, such as algorithmic biases, data privacy concerns, and the misuse of automated feedback, thereby supporting the safe and responsible use of AI in teaching practices (Celik, 2023; Khosravi et al., 2022; Perkins, 2023). With respect to pedagogical expertise, prior research has emphasized the need for teachers to strategically integrate AI technologies with traditional instructional approaches to foster personalized, adaptive, and engaging learning environments (Kshetri, 2023; Popenici & Kerr, 2017). This integration requires not only an understanding of how AI can support differentiated instruction but also the ability to make informed, pedagogical choices during lesson planning. For example, the use of AI-powered learning analytics enables teachers to monitor stu- dents’ progress more precisely and tailor instruction to meet diverse students’ needs (Holmes et al., 2023; Holstein et al., 2019). To support pedagogical integration, Celik (2023) introduced the Intelligent-TPACK framework, an extension of the traditional TPACK framework that in- tegrates AI-specific pedagogical and technological knowledge. This framework offers a conceptual basis for the meaningful incorporation of AI into curriculum design. In addition, pedagogical expertise encom- passes the ability to design innovative, AI-enhanced learning activities. For instance, Lee et al. (2023) proposed a collaborative instructional approach using an AI speaker to facilitate group-based learning, which significantly enhanced student engagement and academic performance. Regarding teaching practice, the integration of AI technologies provides teachers with access to rich data and real-time feedback, thereby facilitating continuous instructional refinement. By analyzing students’ learning data provided by AI systems, teachers can more accurately assess students’ learning outcomes and make timely adjust- ments to their teaching practices (Abulibdeh et al., 2024; Fariani et al., 2023; Fontaine et al., 2019; Lampos et al., 2021). Educational data an- alytics empower teachers to transition from intuition-based teaching to evidence-informed instructional design, enabling the delivery of more differentiated, responsive, and student-centred learning experiences. Recent findings emphasize that experienced instructors who engage deeply with analytics tools integrate both technical and pedagogical knowledge by using dashboards not just for performance monitoring, but also to align course design with diverse learner needs (Li et al., 2025).

This data-informed approach not only enhances teaching effective- ness but also strengthens teachers’ decision-making capacity. For 

example, Zhu et al. (2023) developed an AI-based model for analyzing students’ learning behaviors to predict their academic performance, thereby enabling teachers to implement target instructional in- terventions that improve teaching effectiveness. Such models illustrate how educational data analytics can be integrated into everyday teaching practices, supporting formative assessment, early warning systems, and real-time scaffolding. As teachers become more adept at using educa- tional data analytics tools, they concurrently develop professional competencies in interpreting data, evaluating evidence, and applying insights to instructional design. This process expands the pedagogical function of analytics from a monitoring tool to a driver of transformative learning design. Empirical evidence indicates that when teachers receive structured data literacy training, their capacity to apply insights from educational data analytics to pedagogical decision-making improves significantly (Sandoval-Ríos et al., 2025).

To date, most research has focused on the use of AI for instructional support and on the development of teachers’ technological proficiency with AI tools, commonly referred to as AI competency (Chiu et al., 2024). The TPACK framework has served as a foundational model for enhancing teachers’ pedagogical knowledge development in technology-integrated teaching environments (Celik, 2023; Ning et al., 2024). While prior studies have examined the relationship between TPACK and teaching performance (Aktas¸ & Ozmen, ¨ 2020; Singerin, 2022; Tosuntas¸ et al., 2021), the complex interrelationships among AI competency, TPACK, and teaching performance remain both theoreti- cally underdeveloped and empirically underexplored.

This study seeks to address this gap by offering three key contribu- tions. First, it examines the direct relationships among AI competency, TPACK, and teaching performance. Second, it explores the mediating role of TPACK in the relationship between AI competency and teaching performance. Third, it provides empirical evidence to inform both theoretical development and practical applications in teacher profes- sional development within the context of AI in education.

## 2. Literature review

### _2.1._ _Artificial intelligence (AI) competency_

Artificial intelligence (AI) in computer science aims to create intel- ligent systems capable of decision-making, speech recognition, image perception, and other activities typically requiring human intelligence. The rapid advancement of AI technologies in recent years has signifi- cantly impacted the field of education (Tan et al., 2025). Most contemporary research on AI in education has focused on the concept of AI literacy. According to Long and Magerko (2020), AI literacy refers to a set of knowledge and skills necessary for individuals to utilize AI in various contexts, communicate and collaborate effectively with AI, and critically evaluate AI technologies. Ng et al. (2021) further emphasized that AI literacy also encompasses an understanding of the ethical di- mensions associated with AI applications, particularly in fostering learners’ abilities to use AI technologies ethically. However, Chiu et al. (2024) distinguished between literacy and competency, arguing that while literacy primarily involves understanding specific knowledge, competency emphasizes the effective application of that knowledge. They define AI competency as an individual’s ability to properly explain the concepts and impacts of AI, and to apply AI technologies ethically, effectively, and beneficially.

Given that the aim of this study is to explore teachers’ effective use of AI technologies to enhance teaching performance, AI competency was selected as the central construct. In terms of measuring AI literacy or AI competency, several instruments have been developed in previous research. Hornberger et al. (2023) designed an AI literacy test based on Long and Magerko’s (2020) framework, employing multiple-choice questions to assess students’ understanding of fundamental AI technol- ogies and ethical considerations. Similarly, Ng et al. (2024) developed an AI literacy questionnaire that measures students’ AI literacy across 

four dimensions: affect, behavior, cognition, and ethics. From the perspective of teacher expertise, Celik (2023) created a scale to measure teachers’ competencies in using AI technologies for teaching and learning. This scale, grounded in the TPACK framework, evaluates five dimensions: technological knowledge (TK), technological pedagogical knowledge (TPK), technological content knowledge (TCK), technolog- ical pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK), and ethics (ETH). Although research on AI in education remains in its early stages, previous studies offer a valuable foundation for this study. Chiu et al.’s (2024) conceptualization of AI competency clarifies the focus of this study on teachers’ ability to effectively use AI in instructional settings. Furthermore, Celik’s (2023) study offers a relevant reference for measuring teachers’ AI competency in this context.

### _2.2._ _TPACK framework_

In the 21st century, with the continuous development of information and communication technologies (ICT), education has increasingly transitioned into the digital era. Teachers’ ICT competencies have become a fundamental prerequisite for the digital transformation of education. Building on the integration of ICT with pedagogical content knowledge (PCK), Mishra and Koehler (2006) proposed the technolog- ical pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK) framework to help edu- cators understand the complex interplay among technology, pedagogy, and subject content. Subsequent empirical studies have investigated the validity and structure of the TPACK framework. For instance, Arch- ambault and Barnett (2010) employed a 24-item survey and conducted factor analysis to examine the dimensional structure of TPACK. Simi- larly, Chai et al. (2011) surveyed 834 pre-service teachers and utilized t-tests and structural equation modelling (SEM) to further explore the internal structure of TPACK.

Since the introduction of the TPACK framework, a substantial body of research has focused on measuring TPACK levels. Koehler et al. (2012) conducted a systematic review of TPACK measurement ap- proaches. By analyzing 66 studies, they classified a total of 141 in- struments into five categories: self-report measures, open-ended questionnaires, performance assessments, interviews, and observations. Their findings revealed that while early studies predominantly relied on self-report measures, more recent research has increasingly shifted to- ward performance assessments and observational methods. They emphasized that a framework for integrating technology into teaching should be valued only if it demonstrates a tangible impact on teaching practices. They also noted that performance assessments offer a more accurate evaluation of teaching practices than self-reported data. Similarly, Xu et al. (2013) reviewed 19 studies on TPACK assessment conducted between 2005 and 2013. They categorized the assessment methods into four groups: open-ended questionnaires, interviews, self-assessments, and observations. Xu et al. (2013) noted that although self-assessment was the most widely used method during the early stages of TPACK research, there has been a growing trend toward hybrid ap- proaches that combine both quantitative and qualitative methods in recent years.

Overall, the measurement of TPACK has increasingly adopted multi- method approaches. Recent studies commonly combine self-assessments with performance assessments, interviews, and observations to more effectively evaluate the effects of TPACK on teaching performance. These studies provide valuable insights for the present study, particu- larly in measuring changes in teachers’ TPACK after participating in AI competency training programmes.

### _2.3._ _Teaching performance_

Teaching performance refers to a set of teacher behaviors that align with the educational objectives and pedagogical goals of a course. Evaluating teaching performance enables the assessment of instructional effectiveness and classroom efficiency (Darling-Hammond, 2010; 

Goodman et al., 2008). Through performance evaluation, teachers can identify their strengths and areas for improvement, and make informed adjustments to their instructional objectives, content, and methods in future lessons (Timpson & Andrew, 1997). Therefore, teaching perfor- mance evaluation plays a vital role in supporting teachers’ professional development and enhancing instructional quality.

The United States has been a pioneer in developing performance- based teacher evaluation systems. A prominent example is the Perfor- mance Assessment for California Teachers (PACT), developed by the University of California, Berkeley, in collaboration with a consortium of 12 Californian universities. PACT employes two modes of assessment: embedded assessment, which evaluates pre-service teachers during coursework, and teaching practice assessment, which evaluates teaching performance in real classroom settings. In contrast to traditional self- report surveys, PACT adopts a multi-method approach that includes portfolio evaluations, video analysis of classroom teaching, and assess- ments of student learning outcomes (Pecheone & Chung, 2006). Inspired by PACT, many countries have developed national teacher evaluation frameworks. For example, Ontario, Canada, introduced the Performance Appraisal of New Teachers (PANT), which assesses pre- service teachers across five components: subject knowledge, teaching practice, professional accountability, teamwork, and continuous devel- opment (Larsen, 2009). Similarly, Malaysia adopted a national evalua- tion model based on PACT, focusing on four components: lesson planning, teaching, student evaluation, and teacher reflection (Gallant & Mayer, 2012).

Despite its contributions, PACT has been critiqued for its limited generalizability and inadequacy in supporting teachers’ professional development across the span of their careers (Darling-Hammond, 2010). In response, the United States introduced the Educative Teacher Per- formance Assessment (edTPA), which evaluates teaching performance across three components: planning, teaching and assessment (Sato, 2014). The planning component examines pre-service teachers’ instructional design, course materials, and assessment plans. The teaching component evaluates teaching performance through classroom video analysis focusing on learning outcomes, classroom environment, and instructional methods. The assessment component evaluates how teachers use student learning data to refine instructional practices, drawing on evidence such as student work samples and assessment feedback.

Another influential system is the Danielson Teacher Assessment System (TAS). Unlike edTPA, which primarily targets pre-service teachers, the Danielson model is applicable to teachers across all career stages and is often used for professional mentoring and peer su- pervision (Danielson & McGreal, 2000). This system includes 22 eval- uation indicators grouped into four dimensions: planning and preparation, classroom environment, instruction, and professional re- sponsibilities (Danielson, 2007). Evaluations typically involve class- room observations, supplemented by lesson plans, instructional arrangements, student work samples, portfolios, and interviews. In recent years, attention has shifted toward more diversified and inclusive approaches to teaching performance evaluation. From a methodological standpoint, Sun et al. (2021) proposed a comprehensive evaluation model based on type-II fuzzy sets, assessing university teachers across five dimensions: teaching attitudes, content quality, instructional methods, professionalism, and teaching effects. In terms of evaluation subjects, Carlucci et al. (2018) underscored the importance of student involvement in assessing teaching performance, contrasting this with traditional expert-driven approaches. They argued that, as primary recipients of instruction, students provide critical insights for improving teaching quality. Furthermore, Galvez Suarez and Milla Toro ´

(2018) advocated for aligning evaluation criteria with the broader pol- icy and political contexts of each educational system, rather than focusing exclusively on classroom-based teaching metrics. In sum, teaching performance evaluation is essential not only for assessing the outcomes of teacher professional development but also for 

guiding continuous instructional improvement. In this study, teaching performance serves as a key outcome variable, used to evaluate the effectiveness of classroom instruction following the enhancement of teachers’ AI competency and TPACK levels.

## 3. Research design

### _3.1._ _Research hypotheses_

Recent advances in AI have underscored the growing need to examine how teachers can effectively leverage AI technologies to enhance educational practices. While existing research has begun to explore the relevance of AI competency in teaching, a comprehensive review of the literature reveals persistent gaps in understanding the interrelationships among teachers’ AI competency, TPACK, and teach- ing performance. Although prior studies have explored the link between AI competency and TPACK (e.g., Dogan et al., 2025; Karatas¸ & Ataç, 2025), there remains a lack of empirical evidence examining how these two constructs jointly influence teaching performance in practice. Moreover, while earlier studies suggest that teachers with higher levels of TPACK tend to demonstrate greater willingness and ability to integrate AI tools into their teaching, emerging research indicates that AI competency may serve as a critical antecedent to TPACK develop- ment. For instance, recent empirical findings show that teachers’ AI competency has a significant and positive effect on their TPACK, and may indirectly shape their intentions to design AI-assisted learning through the mediating role of TPACK (Altawalbeh & Al-Said, 2025; Wang et al., 2024).

Despite these findings, there remains a need for empirical validation of the relationships among AI competency, TPACK, and teaching per- formance, particularly within a single, unified model. To address these research gaps, the present study proposes and tests a conceptual model (see [Fig. 1)](#3-research-design) that examines the impact of teachers’ AI competency on their TPACK and teaching performance. Specifically, we investigate whether improvements in AI competency contribute to enhanced TPACK, which in turn may positively influence teaching performance. Based on the theoretical foundation and review of prior research, the following hy- potheses are proposed. 

**H1**. AI competency significantly influences TPACK.

**H2**. TPACK significantly influences teaching performance.

**H3**. AI competency significantly influences teaching performance.

**H4**. TPACK mediates the relationship between AI competency and teaching performance.

### _3.2._ _Participants_

This study employed a purposive sampling strategy to recruit 247 university teachers from a university in Yunnan, China. This university is currently undergoing a digital transformation in education and en- courages the integration of AI technologies to enhance teaching and learning. As part of this initiative, teachers were granted considerable autonomy in selecting specific types of AI applications for the design and 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 1.** Conceptual model.

delivery of their courses, based on their subject area, instructional goals, and teaching preferences. They were also allowed to independently determine when, how, and to what extent AI technologies were incor- porated into their teaching practices.

Although this study was conducted in a naturalistic observational setting where the use of AI tools was neither prescribed nor standard- ized, participating teachers reported a variety of AI-supported instruc- tional applications. These included using AI to generate or revise instructional materials, differentiate learning tasks to meet diverse stu- dent needs, and facilitate feedback and evaluation. In addition, teachers had discretion over how students interacted with AI in learning activ- ities. For example, some allowed students to use AI for in-class question answering, project development, or AI-assisted code writing. The sample was selected to ensure broad representation across pro- fessional titles, disciplinary backgrounds, and years of teaching experi- ence. Participants included Teaching Assistants, Lecturers, Associate Professors, and Professors. They represented a diverse range of academic disciplines, including Arts, Economics, Education, Engineering, History, Law, Literature, Management, and Science. To capture variation across different career stages, teaching experience was categorized into seven groups based on years of teaching, ranging from 1–5 years to 31–35 years.

### _3.3._ _Instruments_

To gain a comprehensive understanding of teachers’ AI competency, TPACK levels, and teaching performance, this study employed a mixed- methods approach incorporating both questionnaire surveys and class- room observations. Teachers’ AI competency and TPACK levels were assessed using validated self-report questionnaires, while teaching per- formance was evaluated through systematic, rubric-based classroom observations. In addition, the questionnaire collected information on the specific AI technologies used by teachers in their teaching practices. During the classroom observation, teachers’ use of AI technologies in teaching was also observed and documented.

#### _3.3.1._ _AI competency scale_

Teachers’ AI competency was measured using the Intelligent-TPACK scale developed by Celik (2023), which evaluates teachers’ knowledge and skills related to AI-based instruction. The scale consists of 27 items distributed across five dimensions: intelligent technology knowledge (AITK; 5 items), intelligent technological pedagogical knowledge (AITPK; 7 items), intelligent technological content knowledge (AITCK; 4 items), intelligent technological pedagogical content knowledge (AIT- PACK; 7 items), and ethics (ETH; 4 items). These dimensions collectively capture the competencies required for effective instruction in AI-integrated educational environments. Items were rated on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 7 (Strongly Agree), with higher scores indicating greater levels of AI competency. The overall Cronbach’s alpha coefficients for this scale exceeded 0.85 across all dimensions, demonstrating high internal consistency. Celik (2023) developed this instrument to address the lack of research surrounding teachers’ application of AI tools for instructional purposes in the class- room. Grounded in the TPACK framework, the scale specifically targets the instructional use of AI technologies.

#### _3.3.2._ _TPACK scale_

Teachers’ TPACK levels were measured using the scale developed by Schmid et al. (2020), which is widely recognized for its reliability and validity in educational research. The scale comprises 28 items, evenly distributed across seven dimensions, each consisting of four items: technological knowledge (TK), pedagogical knowledge (PK), content knowledge (CK), pedagogical content knowledge (PCK), technological content knowledge (TCK), technological pedagogical knowledge (TPK), and technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK). The orig- inal version of the scale utilized a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 

(Strongly Disagree) to 5 (Strongly Agree). Schmid et al. (2020) reported strong internal consistency across all subscales, with Cronbach’s alpha coefficients ranging from 0.77 to 0.91 and McDonald’s omega values ranging from 0.79 to 0.92. These results confirm the scale’s reliability and construct validity for assessing teachers’ TPACK. To ensure consis- tency with the AI competency scale used in this study, the response format was adapted to a 7-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 7 (Strongly Agree), with higher scores indicating higher levels of TPACK.

#### _3.3.3._ _Teaching performance evaluation_

Teaching performance in this study was assessed using the Danielson Teacher Evaluation System (Danielson, 2007), a widely adopted and empirically supported framework for evaluating instructional effec- tiveness across diverse educational contexts. The system comprises four domains, 22 components and 76 elements, each assessed using a four-point rubric scale. The four domains include planning and prepa- ration (Perf1), classroom environment (Perf2), instruction (Perf3), and professional responsibilities (Perf4). The planning and preparation domain evaluates teachers’ planning of instructional content, formula- tion of learning objectives, selection of instructional strategies and re- sources, and overall instructional design. The classroom environment domain assesses the quality of teacher-student interactions, the estab- lishment of a respectful and inclusive learning climate, and classroom management strategies. The instruction domain focuses on communi- cation clarity, questioning and discussion techniques, student engage- ment strategies, formative and summative assessment practices, and the provision of constructive feedback. The professional responsibilities domain measures teachers’ reflective practices, record-keeping and documentation, professional communication, collaboration with col- leagues, participation in professional development, and adherence to ethical and institutional responsibilities. Teaching performance was rated using scoring criteria aligned with clearly defined performance indicators for each domain. Each domain was assigned a maximum score of four points, reflecting the highest level of instructional proficiency.

### _3.4._ _Data collection and analysis_

Data on teachers’ AI competency and TPACK levels were collected through questionnaires administered between November 2023 and December 2024. A total of 247 valid responses were obtained, yielding a 100 % valid response rate.

To assess teaching performance, classroom observations were con- ducted concurrently with the questionnaire administration. The obser- vation period extended from December 2024 to March 2025, with each session lasting approximately one hour. During each observation, three trained observers independently evaluated teaching performance using a standardized rubric based on the Danielson Teacher Evaluation System (Danielson, 2007). The mean score across the three observers was calculated for each domain of teaching performance to enhance objec- tivity and consistency.

Data analysis was conducted using RStudio, a comprehensive sta- tistical software environment that supports data processing, advanced statistical testing, and structural modelling through a broad array of packages and tools. The analysis proceeded in three stages. First, descriptive statistics were computed to explore the distribution of par- ticipants by professional titles, disciplinary backgrounds, and years of teaching experience. In addition, basic statistical summaries and cor- relation coefficients were calculated to examine the relationships among AI competency, TPACK, and teaching performance. To further explore group-level differences, analysis of variance (ANOVA) tests were con- ducted to assess whether teachers’ AI competency varied significantly across different demographic characteristics. Second, the measurement model was validated using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to eval- uate the structural validity of the three-factor model comprising the AI competency scale, the TPACK scale, and the teaching performance 

evaluation rubric. Finally, the study hypotheses were tested using structural equation modelling (SEM) to assess both the direct and indi- rect effects among the three core constructs. This analysis also examined the mediating role of TPACK in the relationship between AI competency and teaching performance.

## 4. Research results

### _4.1._ _Descriptive statistics and correlation analysis_

#### _4.1.1._ _Teachers’ demographics_

To examine the demographic characteristics of the participants, including professional titles, disciplinary backgrounds, and years of teaching experience, descriptive statistical analysis was conducted based on the valid questionnaire data. The results are illustrated in [Figs. 2–4.](#333-teaching-performance-evaluation)

Among the 247 teachers surveyed, 59.11 % held senior professional titles (Associate Professor or Professor). This relatively high proportion suggests that teachers with higher academic ranks at the university may be more actively involved in exploring the integration of AI technologies into their teaching practices. In terms of disciplinary background, the highest representations came from Law, Literature, Management, and Science, followed by Engineering and Economics. In contrast, teachers from Arts, Education, and History were less represented. These trends may reflect disciplinary differences in interest or engagement with AI- powered teaching methods. Regarding years of teaching experience, the distribution across different experience groups was relatively balanced. However, participation among teachers with more than 25 years of experience was notably lower. This pattern suggests that early- and mid-career educators are more inclined to explore AI applications in education, whereas more experienced educators may demonstrate relatively lower levels of engagement with emerging technologies. In addition, the questionnaire investigated which AI tools were being used by teachers. The results are presented in Table 1. Among those who reported using AI tools (99.6 % of the respondents), ERNIE (17.56 %), Kimi (15.50 %), and DeepSeek (14.48 %) were the most commonly used, together accounting for nearly half of the total tool usage. This trend highlights the strong preference for Chinese large language models among domestic teachers. Although ChatGPT accounted for only 5.54 %, it still maintains a notable presence. It is also worth noting that the usage rates of specific applications such as VR (1.54 %), knowledge graph (1.33 %), AI-driven research tool (0.72 %), AI-driven search tool (0.62 %), AI-driven learning and assessment system (0.31 %), AI-driven office software (0.21 %), and text-to-image/video tool (0.10 %) were all below 2 %. This suggests that teachers are currently more focused on conversational AI tools, while the adoption of AI in more specialized or advanced educational scenarios, such as teaching research, learning assessment, and immersive scene simulation, remains limited and exploratory.

### _4.3._ _Confirmatory factor analysis_

A two-step modelling strategy was adopted to examine the latent structural regression model, following the guidelines recommended by Kline (2023). To evaluate the structural validity of the proposed three-factor model—comprising the AI competency scale (AI), the TPACK scale (TPA), and the teaching performance evaluation rubric (Prf)—a confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was conducted. The initial CFA results indicated suboptimal model fit: χ[^2](101) = 657.261, _p \<_ 0.001, SRMR = 0.044, RMSEA = 0.149, TLI = 0.890, CFI = 0.907 (see [Fig. 7)](#43-confirmatory-factor-analysis), suggesting that the hypothesized factor structure required refinement. Based on modification indices, the measurement model was re-specified by allowing the error terms of PK to correlate with CK, PCK, and TCK. Additional correlated error terms were specified between CK and PCK, CK and TK, AITPACK and ETH, AITK and AIT- PACK, and TCK and TPCK (see [Fig. 8)](#5-discussion). These modifications were theo- retically justifiable, likely reflecting unmodeled shared variance arising from conceptual overlap or measurement artifacts. For example, the correlations between the error terms of PK and CK, PCK and TCK may result from overlapping content or shared method variance in the measurement of these constructs. Similarly, the error covariances be- tween CK and PCK, CK and TK, AITPACK and ETH, AITK and AITPACK, and TCK and TPCK may indicate the presence of latent conceptual or contextual similarities not fully accounted for in the original three-factor model.

Following these modifications, the model fit improved substantially, with all overall goodness-of-fit indices indicating an acceptable to excellent fit: χ[^2](93) = 221.018, _p \<_ 0.001, SRMR = 0.036, RMSEA = 0.075, TLI = 0.972, CFI = 0.979. These results provide strong empirical support for the adequacy of the revised three-factor model with specified 

**Fig. 7.**

error covariances for subsequent hypothesis testing. Compared to the initial model, the revised model offers a more nuanced and accurate representation of the interrelationships among the constructs. For example, allowing the error terms of PK to correlate with CK, PCK, and TCK acknowledges that pedagogical knowledge is not independent of but interacts significantly with content and technological knowledge. Likewise, the additional correlated error terms, such as those between CK and PCK, CK and TK, AITPACK and ETH, AITK and AITPACK, and TCK and TPCK, highlight potential conceptual or methodological over- laps, suggesting shared variance not captured by the initial model specification.

By incorporating these modifications, the revised model more effectively captures the complex nature of the relationships among AI competency, TPACK, and teaching performance. Consequently, it pro- vides a more robust foundation for examining how AI competency and TPACK interact to influence teaching performance.

### _4.4._ _Hypothesis testing results_

In the second phase of analysis, structural equation modelling (SEM) was employed to test the hypothesized relationships among teachers’ AI competency, TPACK, and teaching performance. This approach enabled the assessment of both direct and indirect effects, as summarized in [Table 7.](#5-discussion)

[H1:](#3-research-design) AI competency significantly influences TPACK. The direct effect of AI competency on TPACK was significant, with a standardized path coefficient of _β_ = 0.821, _t_ = 15.540, _p \<_ 0.001, providing strong support for Hypothesis [H1.](#3-research-design)

[H2:](#3-research-design) TPACK significantly influences teaching performance. TPACK had a significant positive effect on teaching performance, with a standardized path coefficient of _β_ = 0.590, _t_ = 5.723, _p \<_ 0.001, thereby supporting Hypothesis [H2.](#3-research-design)

## 5. Discussion

Drawing on data collected through questionnaire surveys and classroom observations of 247 university teachers, this study investi- gated the relationships among teachers’ AI competency, TPACK, and teaching performance. Unlike prior studies that focused exclusively on 

| Hypothesis | Hypothesized path | _β_ | SE | _t_ | _p_ | Result |

| [H1](#3-research-design) | AI Competency → TPACK | 0.821 | 0.049 | 15.540 | _\<_0.01 | Supported |
| [H2](#3-research-design) | TPACK → Teaching performance | 0.590 | 0.032 | 5.723 | _\<_0.01 | Supported |
| [H3](#3-research-design) | AI Competency → Teaching Performance (direct effect) | 0.047 | 0.031 | 0.436 | 0.663 | Not Supported |

assessing teachers’ AI competency, this research advances the field by embedding such competency within a TPACK-mediated performance pathway. Specifically, this study posits that teachers’ AI competency influences their TPACK, which in turn leads to improved teaching per- formance. This approach addresses a critical gap in the literature by providing a more nuanced understanding of how teachers’ AI compe- tency translates into effective, technology-enhanced pedagogical prac- tices in higher education.

The analysis yielded four major findings. First, teachers’ AI compe- tency exerted a significant positive effect on their TPACK. This suggests that teachers with stronger capabilities in understanding and applying AI technologies are better positioned to integrate technological, peda- gogical and content knowledge. Such integration is essential for effec- tively navigating diverse learning environments. Teachers with high AI competency are more adept at leveraging digital tools to assess student needs and tailor instructional strategies accordingly, thereby enhancing their overall TPACK levels.

Second, TPACK was found to significantly and positively influence teaching performance. Teachers with higher levels of TPACK are more capable of designing and delivering instruction that integrates technol- ogy, pedagogy, and content knowledge in their teaching practices. This integration aligns with the principles of constructivist pedagogy, which advocates for learners to actively construct knowledge through mean- ingful interaction with digital tools and real-world contexts. By equip- ping teachers with the ability to design adaptive, learner-centred environments, TPACK-informed instruction fosters deeper engagement and promotes authentic learning experiences (Do et al., 2023). Third, the direct effect of AI competency on teaching performance was not statistically significant. This finding underscores the pivotal role of TPACK as a mediating construct in this relationship. Although tech- nical proficiency in AI is a necessary condition for integrating advanced technologies into teaching, it is not sufficient on its own. The effec- tiveness of AI integration depends on a teacher’s ability to contextualize and apply AI tools within pedagogical strategies and content-specific frameworks. In other words, the effective translation of AI competency into improved teaching performance requires its operationalization through pedagogical expertise and disciplinary knowledge—core com- ponents of the TPACK framework.

Fourth, the results confirmed that AI competency positively in- fluences teaching performance through the mediating effect of TPACK. Teachers who enhance their AI competency, for example by mastering intelligent teaching tools, become more proficient at integrating AI technologies into instructional design. This proficiency strengthens their TPACK levels, ultimately leading to enhanced teaching performance and better student learning outcomes.

Based on the analysis of teachers’ AI competency and TPACK, this study further examined the structural distinctions between AI compe- tency and the traditional TPACK framework. While traditional TPACK emphasizes integrating technology, pedagogy, and content knowledge, AI competency highlights the unique characteristics and growing importance of AI within this framework (Karatas¸ & Ataç, 2025). Spe- cifically, intelligent technology knowledge emerges as a distinct and critical dimension within AI competency, encompassing teachers’ con- ceptual understanding and applied mastery of AI technologies. This differentiation reflects the evolving instructional demands of the AI era, where effective teaching requires not only general technological inte- gration but also specialized knowledge of AI to meaningfully enhance student learning. Teachers proficient in AI concepts can more effectively leverage intelligent instructional tools to provide individualized learning support—a capability not sufficiently addressed within the traditional TPACK framework (Celik, 2023; Ning et al., 2024). Furthermore, incorporating an ethics dimension within the Intelligent-TPACK framework significantly expands the scope of teach- ers’ professional competencies. The widespread adoption of AI tech- nologies in education has heightened ethical concerns related to algorithmic bias, data privacy, and students’ emotional and moral 

development (Celik, 2023). This study found that the ethics dimension significantly influences teachers’ fulfillment of their professional re- sponsibilities (_t_ = 6.238, _p \<_ 0.001). Specifically, teachers who exhibi- ted greater ethical awareness about AI were more likely to prioritize student data privacy, safeguard the security of personal information, and critically monitor AI systems for algorithmic bias to prevent ineq- uitable student evaluation and treatment. Additionally, ethically literate teachers proactively guided students in developing responsible attitudes toward AI use, thereby promoting moral responsibility and fostering appropriate ethical values (Celik, 2023; Fassbender, 2024; Grajeda et al., 2023; Williams, 2024). Collectively, these findings extend the conceptualization of teachers’ professional responsibilities, highlighting ethical literacy as a central element of teachers’ professional develop- ment in the AI era.

Moreover, data from questionnaires and classroom observations revealed a notable implementation gap. Although 99.6 % of teachers reported using AI tools, only 53.44 % (n = 132) were observed actually integrating AI into their classroom practice. This indicates a clear discrepancy between high levels of adoption intention and relatively low levels of classroom implementation. One possible explanation is that teachers primarily use conversational AI to generate instructional de- signs, teaching materials, test questions, and related content. These ac- tivities typically take place outside of class time and are not directly observable during classroom sessions. As a result, such uses can gener- ally be inferred from teachers’ lesson plans and reflective documentation.

Overall, the observation data indicate that teachers’ in-class appli- cation of AI remains concentrated at the substitution–augmentation levels, and has yet to reach the modification–redefinition stages of technology integration (Song et al., 2025). This insight informs the design of professional development programmes that emphasize the pedagogical potential of AI at more advanced levels of integration. Specifically, it advocates for a shift toward pedagogical approaches that leverage AI to support metacognitive skill-building, reflective learning, and student autonomy. These are key principles of self-regulated learning in higher education (Lan & Zhou, 2025). Looking ahead, AI can evolve from a peripheral tool into a core driver of instructional innovation by enhancing support for instructional design, reforming evaluation mechanisms, and developing robust data ecosystems.

## 6. Limitations and future work

Although this study provides important insights into the relation- ships among teachers’ AI competency, TPACK, and teaching perfor- mance, several limitations must be acknowledged.

First, this study employed a cross-sectional research design, which captures relationships among variables at a single point in time. This design limits the ability to infer causality and assess changes over time in teachers’ competencies and practices. Since the development of teach- ers’ AI competency is inherently a dynamic and continuous process, its impact on TPACK and teaching performance likely evolves over time. Future research should therefore adopt longitudinal designs to track teachers’ AI competency, TPACK development, and teaching perfor- mance across multiple time points. Such studies would provide richer, more causal insights and deepen the understanding of the develop- mental trajectories and long-term impacts of AI competency on teaching practices.

Second, evaluations of teaching performance in this study relied primarily on subjective assessments, which can introduce potential bias. While utilizing a scientifically validated rubric grounded in the Dan- ielson framework reduced some risks, subjective judgments remain vulnerable to individual preferences, observer interpretations, and contextual variability. These factors may compromise the objectivity, consistency, and accuracy of performance evaluations, potentially affecting the reliability of the study’s findings.

To address this limitation, future research could explore the 

integration of intelligent learning analytics systems into teaching per- formance evaluations. Such systems would enable more objective as- sessments by analyzing student achievement data, learning behaviors, and engagement metrics collected from digital learning platforms (Alotaibi & Alshehri, 2023; Banihashem et al., 2022; Chaudhry et al., 2023; Crompton & Burke, 2023; Li et al., 2022; Zawacki-Richter et al., 2019). These systems represent an emerging area of educational data analytics, with the potential to reshape traditional evaluation practices by making them more dynamic, real-time, and learner-responsive. Incorporating these objective measures would significantly reduce subjective biases, thereby enhancing the reliability and validity of evaluations.

Future research should also investigate how teachers interpret and act upon these analytics to inform pedagogical strategies. Understanding this interpretive process is crucial for designing effective educational data analytics dashboards, training teachers in data literacy, and avoiding potential misuse or overreliance on automated indicators. In this way, educational data analytics not only supports teacher accountability and performance assessment but also serves as a peda- gogical tool for continuous instructional improvement. Moving toward comprehensive, data-informed evaluation frameworks represents a promising direction for facilitating teachers’ successful adaptation to AI- enhanced educational environments.

## 7. Conclusion

This study examined the relationships among teachers’ AI compe- tency, TPACK, and teaching performance. The findings revealed that AI competency significantly and positively influences TPACK, that TPACK substantially enhances teaching performance, and that TPACK mediates the relationship between AI competency and teaching performance. These results provide empirical validation of the pivotal role of inte- grated technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge in enhancing teaching effectiveness within AI-enhanced learning environments. As AI technologies become increasingly embedded in education, they present both new opportunities and heightened expectations for teach- ers’ professional development. While AI expands the instructional tools and resources available to teachers, it also necessitates rethinking and redefining teachers’ professional competencies. Beyond mastery of disciplinary content and traditional pedagogical skills, teachers must now cultivate a deep conceptual and practical expertise in AI technol- ogies and strategically integrate them into their teaching practices. This study underscores that effective professional development in the AI era requires both technological empowerment and pedagogical trans- formation as critical and complementary dimensions.

On one hand, technological empowerment emerges as a vital goal for teachers’ professional development. Teachers must proactively acquire competencies in areas such as machine learning, educational data ana- lytics, and the utilization of AI-enhanced instructional tools. These competencies provide teachers with essential technological proficiency, 

Therefore, fostering a teacher-centred professional development ecosystem that emphasizes AI competency is crucial for enhancing educational quality and long-term sustainability. Establishing such an ecosystem requires collaborative efforts among multiple stakeholders, including governments, educational institutions, schools, and teachers themselves. Through robust policy frameworks, targeted professional development programmes, supportive learning environments, and ongoing competency refinement, stakeholders can cultivate a compre- hensive and dynamic professional development ecosystem. Ultimately, this integrated approach will provide sustained support for teacher growth, innovation, and the continuous advancement of educational practices.

ITPK7. I have the knowledge to select AI-based tools to sustain stu- dents’ motivation.

### _Intelligent TCK_

ITCK1. I can use AI-based tools to search for educational material in my teaching field.

ITCK2. I am aware of various AI-based tools which are used by professionals in my teaching field.

ITCK3. I can use AI-based tools to better understand the contents of my teaching field.

ITCK4. I know how to utilize my field-specific AI-based tools (e.g., intelligent tutor for Math).

### _Intelligent TPACK_

ITPACK1. In teaching my field, I know how to use different AI-based tools for adaptive feedback.

ITPACK2. In teaching my field, I know how to use different AI-based tools for personalized learning.

ITPACK3. In teaching my field, I know how to use different AI-based tools for real-time feedback.

ITPACK4. I can teach a subject using AI-based tools with diverse teaching strategies.

ITPACK5. I can teach lessons that appropriately combine my teach- ing content, AI-based tools, and teaching strategies.

ITPACK6. I can take a leadership role among my colleagues in the integration of AI-based tools into our teaching field.

ITPACK7. I can select various AI-based tools to monitor students’ learning in my teaching process.

### _Ethics_

ETH1. I can assess to what extent AI-based tools consider individual differences (e.g., race and gender) of all students in my teaching. ETH2. I can evaluate to what extent AI-based tools behave fair to all students in my teaching.

ETH3. I can understand the justification of any decision made by an AI-based tool.

ETH4. I can understand who the responsible developers are in the design and decision of AI-based tools.

### _Open-ended Question_

- Please describe the AI tools you have used in your teaching practices.

## Appendix B. TPACK Survey

### _PK_

PK1. I can adapt my teaching based upon what students currently understand or do not understand.

PK2. I can adapt my teaching style to different learners. PK3. I can use a wide range of teaching approaches in a classroom setting.

PK4. I can assess student learning in multiple ways.

### _CK_

CK1. I have sufficient knowledge about my teaching subject. CK2. I can use a subject-specific way of thinking in my teaching subject.

CK3. I know the basic theories and concepts of my teaching subject. CK4. I know the history and development of important theories in my teaching subject.

### _TK_

TK1. I keep up with important new technologies. TK2. I frequently play around with the technology.

TK3. I know about a lot of different technologies. TK4. I have the technical skills I need to use technology.

### _PCK_

PCK1. I know how to select effective teaching approaches to guide student thinking and learning in my teaching subject.

PCK2. I know how to develop appropriate tasks to promote students complex thinking of my teaching subject.

PCK3. I know how to develop exercises with which students can consolidate their knowledge of my teaching subject.

PCK4. I know how to evaluate students’ performance in my teaching subject.

### _TPK_

TPK1. I can choose technologies that enhance the teaching ap- proaches for a lesson.

TPK2. I can choose technologies that enhance students’ learning for a lesson.

TPK3. I can adapt the use of the technologies that I am learning about to different teaching activities.

TPK4. I am thinking critically about how to use technology in my classroom.

### _TCK_

TCK1. I know how technological developments have changed the field of my subject.

TCK2. I can explain which technologies have been used in research in my field.

TCK3. I know which new technologies are currently being developed in the field of my subject.

TCK4. I know how to use technologies to participate in scientific discourse in my field.

### _TPCK_

TPCK1. I can use strategies that combine content, technologies, and teaching approaches that I learned about in my coursework in my classroom.

TPCK2. I can choose technologies that enhance the content for a lesson.

TPCK3. I can select technologies to use in my classroom that enhance what I teach, how I teach, and what students learn.

TPCK4. I can teach lessons that appropriately combine my teaching subject, technologies, and teaching approaches.
